title: The Mets as The People’s Team
author: Daniel Falcone
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/05/metforpeace-680x498.jpg)

[A.M. Gittlitz](https://astrapublishinghouse.com/creator/a-m-
gittlitz-2341553/) is an organizer, writer and the author of _I Want to
Believe: Posadism, UFOs and Apocalypse Communism_. His latest work,
[_Metropolitans: New York Baseball, Class Struggle, and the People’s
Team_](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/808034/metropolitans-by-am-
gittlitz/) (Penguin Random House, 2026), highlights three phases of the
franchise’s history, spanning 1776 to 2005. Part [revisionist
history](https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300283273/the-ever-changing-
past/), part [material
culture](https://sites.udel.edu/materialculture/about/what-is-material-
culture/) study, and part
[ethnography](https://www.culanth.org/fieldsights/more-than-a-game-a-black-
feminist-look-at-the-anthropology-of-sports), Gittlitz manages to capture the
symbolism and essence of Mets fandom in a way that authors before him have
failed to grasp. In [this
book](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2026/03/30/metropolitans-a-m-
gittlitz-book-review), he achieves his goal, which is to “use the Mets’
tragic, comic, and chaotic history to rip open the dead skin of our nation’s
tight-stitched pastime,” while “allowing an alternate history of America.”

_**Daniel Falcone:** What led you to write [the
book](https://www.wsj.com/arts-culture/books/metropolitans-review-when-new-
york-was-metsmerized-2c299f43), and how is it structured? _

**A.M. Gittlitz:** I’ve always had this interest in the Mets that I thought
was maybe a bit idiosyncratic, but not uncommon -- that my love of the team
has a lot more to do with its political, social, and cultural connection to
the left and the working class and the overall [underdog
spirit](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2025/05/12/if-the-mets-are-no-
longer-underdogs-are-they-still-the-mets) of New Yorkers, even more so than
their results on the field.

For example, the moment that I recall being proudest as a Mets fan was in 2020
when [Dominic Smith](https://www.cbssports.com/mlb/news/mets-dominic-smith-
speaks-out-after-jacob-blake-shooting-people-still-dont-care/) led a walk-off
when playing the Florida Marlins following the shooting in Kenosha of [Jacob
Blake](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/federal-officials-close-review-
officer-involved-shooting-jacob-blake) and the subsequent killing of two
protesters. That was part of a [wildcat](https://jacobin.com/2020/08/nba-
strike-lebron-iguodala-milwaukee-bucks) general strike throughout sports that
began in the [NBA](https://www.nytimes.com/2020/08/26/sports/basketball/nba-
boycott-bucks-magic-blake-shooting.html) with the [Milwaukee
Bucks](https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/2025286/2020/08/26/bucks-walkout-in-
support-of-jacob-blake-leads-to-nba-postponing-playoff-games/)and was
relatively slow to spread to baseball. For the Mets to be one of the few teams
to do one of these unpermitted walkouts was incredibly inspiring to me. It
confirmed a lot of what I always loved about the Mets since my fandom began in
the late 90s, when the Mets seemed to be something of a [conscious
rival](https://naacp.org/actions/action-alert-justice-jacob-blake) to Giuliani
and Steinbrenner’s Yankees and John Rocker’s Braves.

I found more evidence when Smith’s walkout was seemingly immortalized in the
[Mets Museum](https://www.mlb.com/mets/ballpark/hospitality/tours/amazin-
artifacts) the next season. But then, another couple of seasons later, that
exhibit for [Dom Smith](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/mets-marlins-walk-off-
field-protest-black-lives-matter/) and the walkout was gone from the [Mets
Museum](https://www.mlb.com/mets/fans/mets-house). I worried Mets fans might
forget about it along with other moments Mets fans have forgotten about or
maybe had a lower priority for in varying [narratives of team
history](https://www.politico.com/story/2007/04/in-ny-is-team-loyalty-a-
partisan-affair-003647). So, I conceived of writing a political narrative of
the team’s history that also theorized why the Mets are a political team after
three different [ownership changes](https://sabr.org/bioproj/topic/new-york-
mets-team-ownership-history/), various eras and rebranding. After all, it is
just a corporate franchise, so, how is it that this team can endure as
political in some way?

The key to that was when I discovered in separate research that the downtown
counterculture and radical milieus in New York during the 60s, the [New
Left](https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-mets-class-struggle-book-interview/)
really loved the Mets. That was the result of the team’s initial branding as
an anti-team to the Yankees and the restoration of the
[Dodgers](https://www.espn.com/blog/new-york/mets/post/_/id/21603/when-giants-
dodgers-left-they-converted) and [Giants](https://www.latimes.com/socal/la-
canada-valley-sun/tsn-vsl-thoughts-from-dr-joe-explaining-connection-to-the-
new-york-mets-20151029-htmlstory.html) as a people’s team, but then also the
way the fan base took on that marketing with a DIY enthusiasm that exceeded
it.

The way I tell the story is a reversed fan history. It begins with a more
sober [Marxist](https://brooklynrail.org/2014/05/field-notes/baseball-and-
marxism-in-brooklyn-and-boston/) reading of the creation of baseball history
through its labor relations and the way the business appealed to different
demographics of fans between the mid-19th century and
[1962](https://www.metsheritage.com/collection/brand-new-in-62-the-first-
season/) when the Mets debuted. As the book goes on and my memories of the
Mets appear in the [90s](https://www.mlb.com/mets/history/timeline-1990s)
chapters moving forward, it becomes a much more subjective fan history where I
can look at something that’s difficult to put into terms: the love a fan has
for their team.

_**Daniel Falcone:** I like how you used a chronological approach and then
went into the thematic political moments to illuminate your own constructions
of the team. To what extent do [the
Mets](https://www.wnyc.org/story/a-peoples-history-of-the-mets/) still carry
the working-class energy that you are trying to capture?_

**A.M. Gittlitz:** When I started writing the book I didn’t know too much
about baseball’s origins. I indeed had an idea that maybe the sport was
invented by the working class. But that turned out to not be true. It was, in
fact, invented by the [upper middle class](https://www.oah.org/process/major-
league-baseballs-historical-quest-to-entice-middle-and-upper-class-fans-to-
the-park-tannenbaum/) in Manhattan.

These were people who worked on Wall Street, accountants, office workers,
paper pushers, doctors, architects, and that made the game make a lot more
sense to me. This wasn’t a sport played by workers in what little downtime
they had, but was a [heavily structured](https://www.history.com/articles/who-
invented-baseball), legalistic, well-designed, well-proportioned, artisanal
game played by office workers dreaming of a yeoman future running free in the
fields of the [American Frontier](https://www.historians.org/resource/the-
significance-of-the-frontier-in-american-history/). That gave me a new
perspective on the sport balanced between this very technical defense – with a
technician (pitcher) throwing an object with this defensive structure behind
him. The [diamond resembles](https://southerncrossreview.org/53/diamond2.htm)
something of a factory or an urban production process, with three guys in a
vast agrarian outfield. Subconsciously this was a
[microcosm](https://jhupress.wordpress.com/2013/04/01/baseball-and-
agrarianism/) of the total social factory. They then take turns maintaining
the production of outs, and then picking up a big stick, smashing the whole
process by running free around the field in a chaotic sabotage of the game’s
banality.

That only became more obvious following the [Civil
War](https://baseballhall.org/discover/baseball-came-of-age-during-civil-war).
The game spread in Union camps, both among Union soldiers and Confederate
prisoners of war, to become the national pastime. The [game
professionalized](https://daily.jstor.org/how-baseball-became-a-profession/)
in the late 1860s, alongside the development of modern industrial relations,
until you see literal workers on the middle-class progenitor’s [idyllic
field](https://baseballhall.org/about-the-hall/history/history-of-doubleday-
field), thus fully appearing as a balanced tension between the desires to
contain and unleash [proletarian
energy](https://digitalcommons.butler.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1428&context=ugtheses).

_**Daniel Falcone:** What makes the [Mets
unique](https://www.justmets.net/p/saying-goodbye-to-the-2024-new-york) as a
franchise?_

**A.M. Gittlitz:** I was influenced by the book of Tony Collins, [_Sport in
Capitalist Society_](https://www.routledge.com/Sport-in-Capitalist-Society-A-
Short-History/Collins/p/book/9780415813563), which rejects a lot of the
previous leftist scholarship arguing sports are corrupted by capitalism. He
argues modern sport and [capitalism](https://theweek.com/articles/448171/how-
modern-capitalism-resegregating-baseball-21st-century) are one and the same,
developed through the same period in the 19th century. Their character as mass
spectacle, however, links the owners and investors with the desire of [worker-
athletes](https://keystoneresearch.org/research_publication/workers-are-
players-too-how-organized-labor-build-major-league-baseball/) and spectators
to overcome their station.

So, when a team, like the sixties’ Mets, or [New Deal-era
Dodgers](https://www.walteromalley.com/dodger-history/us-presidents-and-
dodgers-history/), or the [Gilded-Age
Giants](https://newyorkgiantspreservationsociety.com/), or the Roaring
Twenties’ Yankees puncture the normality of sport as a mere capitalist
enterprise, they become a “[people’s
team](https://jacobin.com/2022/05/baseball-history-labor-civil-rights-
robinson-flood).” They connect the fanbase and the city and the political
moment in a way that theatrically reveals and transcends it. I think all
sports fans, if they’re really being honest with themselves, although they
might complain a lot about players’ privileges, their high salaries, the high-
ticket prices, or put that on the ownership if they’re a little bit left-
oriented, what they really appreciate is when the game breaks down in some
way. Something happens that is above and beyond the normal feature of the
game. Especially in baseball, like, often or most of the time, a very boring
sport.

Before [Babe Ruth](https://baseballhall.org/discover-more/stories/baseball-
history/called-shot), for example, the home run was something of a taboo.
There was a material reason for that – the owners wanted to keep offense low
because the better a player’s offensive stats the more they had to pay them.
So, Ruth, by unleashing the popularity of the long ball, was really hated by
the baseball establishment, but loved by Americans in the way that took
baseball to a new level. The Yankees had to build a massive [new
ballpark](https://www.baberuthcentral.com/babesimpact/babe-ruths-legacy/the-
house-that-ruth-built/), twice the size of most ballparks at the time, to
accommodate new demographics of Ruth’s fans. And it was filled with, for the
first time, working-class people, notably including [Black fans from
Harlem](https://sabr.org/sabr-rucker-archive/ruthba01_02/) who believed that
[Babe Ruth](https://medium.com/buzzer-beater/was-babe-ruth-black-8456f2aabc0d)
might be Black as well. The Dodgers were the next team to achieve this status
with an explosion of attendance following the appearance of Jackie Robinson in
1947. Then the Mets did the same in the 60s by attracting the maturing youth
of the Baby Boom, many of whom were the exurban children of White Flight.

_**Daniel Falcone:** Can you talk about how you frame the history of the teams
in the city? How do you go about comparing the [Mets and the
Yankees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mets%E2%80%93Yankees_rivalry) and how
their followings coincide with competing social issues? _

**A.M. Gittlitz:** The Yankees were born from the American League, which was a
renegade competitor to the National League monopoly formed following the
[Players’ League revolt of
1890](https://www.nebraskapress.unl.edu/nebraska/9780803249417/the-great-
baseball-revolt/). The PL, created by the [first players’
union](https://www.vice.com/en/article/baseballs-forgotten-brotherhood-the-
first-athlete-union-in-american-pro-sports/)organized largely by ex-players of
the 1884 Metropolitans on the Giants, was socialistic and cooperationist, but
failed to challenge the deep pockets of the Gilded-Age NL magnates. In the
aftermath, a Cincinnati sportswriter named [Ban
Johnson](https://baseballhall.org/hall-of-famers/johnson-ban), banned from
baseball for criticizing the NL during the revolt, built the rival AL circuit
as a sort of progressive Republican [trust-
busting](https://sabr.org/journal/article/alito-the-origin-of-the-baseball-
antitrust-exemption/) league, with him serving in the role as a version of
[Teddy Roosevelt](https://www.mlb.com/cut4/teddy-roosevelt-was-scared-of-
baseball). He was a conservative, Midwest Protestant who wanted to restore the
greatness of baseball as a patriotic sport, both in terms of its upper-class
fan culture, but also the way it was organized amongst owners as a collective
of small business owners.

The team he brought to New York, the
[Highlanders](https://stowens.medium.com/before-they-were-
yankees-1f0ec52d5677) (eventually known as the Yankees from an ironic local
nickname), bucked this trend in two ways. One, they played in an Upper
Manhattan park near the Giants’ Polo Grounds and were meant to be the rival to
that now-elite team whose Tammany-linked owner [Andrew
Freedman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Freedman) sought to be the
singular CEO of baseball. Their fans were given little American flags on
Opening Day to signal they were more patriotic, as Johnson hoped the AL would
prove more respectable than the urban degeneracy of big-city machines.

But to be able to get the park built in New York, Johnson had to cut a deal
with a progressive wing of the Machine. The Yankees were put under the control
of a corrupt former police chief and a backroom-saloon owner who gave the
[Yankees](https://www.realclearhistory.com/2014/03/30/why_yankees_benefitted_from_prohibition_4792.html)
a very underworld character in their first two decades. It wasn’t until 1920,
after the team was sold to a New York beer baron whose fortune was threatened
by prohibition, that the Yankees teamed up with the Red Sox to launch what the
press labeled an insurrection against Ban Johnson through the prohibited
acquisition of Babe Ruth and [Carl
Mays](https://sabr.org/journal/article/remembering-carl-mays/). They became an
expression of mass enthusiasm for the omnipotence of capitalism in the Roaring
Twenties. When Babe Ruth had the chance to organize a player’s union early in
the 20s, he declined. This was also something of a populist gesture, because
workers at this time of the class struggle were seen as an anachronism from an
earlier mode of capitalism.

In the 30s, the [Depression](https://scholarworks.uni.edu/facbook/60/) really
woke up the working class to the reality of that arrangement. Without fighting
organizations, all those privileges the bosses and company unions had given
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/05/9781662603006.jpeg)](https://astrapublishinghouse.com/product/metropolitans-9781662603006/)them
are taken away. Massive strike waves break out, filling the ranks of the [AFL,
then the CIO](https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/3573914/2022/09/07/mlbpa-afl-
cio-minor-league-union/). But baseball remains untouched. This was largely
because the player production system, [Branch
Rickey’s](https://www.nysportsday.com/2020/04/11/what-if-branch-rickey-ran-
the-mets-in-1962/) farm system, had indoctrinated mostly Southern ball players
with the ideology of the baseball’s owners. But Rickey began to understand the
limits of this system as it began to generalize throughout the sport and the
labor pool tightened. He wanted to expand the sport
[internationally](https://sabr.org/journal/article/rickeys-folly-how-the-
continental-league-forced-baseball-expansion/) and open the ranks of the
majors to Black and other non-white players. Knowing he could not do this in
St. Louis, he turned to Brooklyn, where the hapless
[Dodgers](https://www.mlb.com/dodgers/history/timeline-1930s) had been reduced
to the stature of the Hooverville “bums” lining the waterfront.

He helped revitalize the team by playing to the working-class unionist
attitude of their fans in several ways, including the adaptation of blue in
what I believe was a nod to [blue-collar
work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue-collar_worker). Finally, he adapted
the [integrationist theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball_color_line)
of the CIO that if Black and white workers could collaborate in the workplace,
then racism would be solved, and the business of baseball could expand to new
frontiers.

Of course, the deeper structural contradictions of race and class deepened
through the fifties, sending the [Giants and
Dodgers](https://www.mlb.com/cut4/why-did-the-dodgers-and-giants-move-to-
california-c303090362) out west alongside hundreds of runaway factories and
the middle-class taxbase. Rickey, along with Mayor Wagner and [Robert
Moses](https://www.qchron.com/editions/queenswide/how-the-mets-came-to-be-
queens-team/article_b68509ef-ba77-50a1-ac17-29ee75541a51.html), fought
baseball to recombine and restore these teams -- as the Mets in 1962 were the
superficial answer to this obvious expression of the deindustrialization
crisis.

While the Mets were a private enterprise run by [Joan
Payson](https://sabr.org/journal/article/joan-whitney-payson-a-pioneer-for-
the-new-york-mets/), who was the wealthiest American woman at the time, they
were also a public project, because they played in a Municipal Stadium in
Flushing championed by Moses as a way of getting his “True Central Park” built
to recenter the city between cosmopolitan Manhattan and metropolitan suburbia.
This [public-private partnership](https://www.mlb.com/press-release/press-
release-amazin-mets-foundation-nyc-parks-and-landtek-partner-to-renovate-b)
was, remarkably, the same populist, philanthropic, urban-expansionist strategy
Tammany had developed by professionalizing and spectacularizing baseball in
the nineteenth century, including funding the original [Metropolitans of
1880](https://sabr.org/bioproj/topic/new-york-metropolitans-team-ownership-
history/). It was no coincidence they chose the same name.

Because Rickey and the Mets would be terrible in their first years, a result
of the expansion draft designed by the owners to ensure they would not be
competitors, he suggested Payson incorporate several [colorful
gimmicks](https://www.nytimes.com/2022/03/23/sports/baseball/mets-60th-
anniversary.html) to attract a new generation of loyal fans. This included
modern features of the ballpark, a comic-book like Pop Art aesthetic, and a
pitch to the New York literati that the Mets would be a technicolor humanist
antidote to grayscale Yankee conservatism. The defining moment of this scheme
came during [1962 Spring
Training](https://www.nytimes.com/2012/02/20/sports/baseball/remembering-the-
mets-first-spring-in-1962.html), when the Mets played against the Yankees.
Although it was an exhibition game, the press dutifully played it up as a
grudge match between an underdog “[people’s
team](https://www.thefanfiles.com/articles/metropolitans-class-struggle-am-
gittlitz)” of washed-up veterans and unknown young journeymen and a decaying
Empire.

_**Daniel Falcone:** You do a great deal of work on identity, resistance and
social movements, especially in the book’s latter stages. Can you elaborate on
the importance of these in the context of Mets history and fandom? The [Civil
Rights movement](https://baseballhall.org/civilrights) comes to mind as an
example. _

**A.M. Gittlitz:** In 1964 the Mets moved into [Shea
Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shea_Stadium), where they began
annually outdrawing the Yankees. Sportswriters begin to wonder, however, how
long the phenomenon of a lovable-loser team could last, especially considering
so many young Mets fans were beginning to be interested in the Civil Rights
Movement and other social issues. Indeed, many Mets fans were a part of these
movements, like [Mickey Schwerner and Andrew
Goodman](https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/freedomsummer-
murder/) who were part of Freedom Summer in Mississippi and were killed, along
with [James Chaney](https://www.fbi.gov/history/famous-cases/mississippi-
burning), by Klansmen sent to allegedly find a “J-boy in a Mets hat.”

Around the same time, [Cleon
Jones](https://www.nytimes.com/2019/06/28/sports/for-cleon-jones-baseball-was-
only-the-beginning.html), Elio Chacon, and other players of the Mets’ [Buffalo
Bisons](https://x.com/BuffaloBisons?s=20) affiliate were sent to play some
games in the South to get fans ready for Hank Aaron and the Braves move from
Milwaukee to Atlanta. Inspired by the [Civil Rights
Movement](https://www.faithandfearinflushing.com/2025/08/18/this-is-the-
ballclub-from-the-age-of-aquarius/), the players reportedly held their own
sit-in for three nights at a Florida restaurant that had refused their
service.

In 1968, the team, now the youngest in baseball, joined a sport-wide boycott
of games before the funeral of [Dr. Martin Luther King,
Jr.](https://x.com/Mets/status/2013280632969814435?s=20), and then one of a
few teams that voted to boycott games before the funeral of [Robert
Kennedy](https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/2021/06/06/rfk-death-mlb-
players-boycott/) later that season. And that really gave the team a
[political reputation](https://newyorkmets.medium.com/cleon-jones-on-mlk-
day-a8b4986a3a07). In 1969, the Mets’ miraculous worst-to-first run attracted
Mets fans who had abandoned sports for revolutionary politics. Incredibly, the
players were on board as well- supporting the candidacy of anti-war mayor
[John Lindsay](https://www.mcny.org/exhibition/americas-mayor), with Tom
Seaver even seemingly dedicating their World Series run to ending the war in
Vietnam.

This was completely unseen in baseball prior. Statements against the war and
U.S. imperialism had been made previously by athletes like [Paul
Robeson](https://www.mlb.com/news/featured/paul-robeson-met-judge-landis-to-
end-baseball-segregation), Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Muhammad Ali, and the ‘[68
Olympic Runners](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/articles/olympic-athletes-who-
took-a-stand-593920/), but no white athletes, and no baseball players. So,
that was an unusual thing to see and do, but it seemed very natural to the
Mets. When Seaver pitched Game 4 of the World Series on [Moratorium
Day](https://www.npr.org/2014/10/15/356435069/baseball-vietnam-and-coming-of-
age-at-the-1969-world-series), cadres of leftist Mets fans pamphleteered
outside the ballpark, a skywriter above Shea wrote “[Stop
War](https://digital.history.pcusa.org/islandora/19688),” and several fans
refused to stand for the National Anthem.

_**Daniel Falcone:** America has returned to a very dark period with a
fascistic leader. How should we navigate sports? We want to avoid feeding
capitalist industry but on the other hand, baseball [can build
community](https://www.weforum.org/stories/2021/01/uniting-the-world-through-
sport-what-can-we-learn-from-sport-in-enabling-social-cohesion/) in your view,
correct?_

**A.M. Gittlitz:** In the Epilogue of the book, I chronicle, day by day, the
Mets’ “OMG Gay [Grimace](https://duquesneduke.org/grimace-and-the-metsthe-
weirdest-team-in-baseball/opinions/)” 2024 season – this gave me the
opportunity to test out the theories of sports, politics, and the Mets as
mediator in real time by going to games, watching the team, interviewing fans,
cataloging the energy at [Citi Field](https://www.mlb.com/mets/ballpark),
while also wondering what this all meant for the moment in the United States,
the looming elections, Biden and then Kamala versus Trump, and the ongoing
suppression of the pro-Palestine movement. I found there were several very
clear parallels.

For one, there had been a protest at Yankee Stadium against the [Yankees’
support of Zionism](https://www.foxnews.com/sports/yankees-mariano-rivera-pro-
israel), both from their front office and from some of the players. Those
activists called for sports fans throughout New York to engage in similar
protests with their team. And while Mets fans likely would have done this,
they couldn’t find any clear enough connection between Steve Cohen and Israel
like the open [Zionism](https://nypost.com/2026/03/02/sports/yankees-harrison-
cohen-embracing-team-israel-honor-for-wbc/) of the Yankees’ organization and
players to protest.

One player on the Mets, [Harrison
Bader](https://www.si.com/fannation/mlb/fastball/news/minnesota-twins-jewish-
outfielder-harrison-bader-commits-to-joining-team-israel-for-2026-world-
baseball-classic-after-missing-2023-tournament-with-oblique-
injury-01jsf0n2ftt8), who had been selected for a team in Israel and ended up
playing for Team Israel in the recent [World Baseball
Classic](https://www.mlb.com/world-baseball-classic), wore a Star of David on
his belt in support of the Israeli hostages in Gaza. But there had been no
other statement by baseball players in support of Palestine. So, that felt,
for a moment, like a bit of a dead end. The clearer political expression
during the season was the embrace of the Mets, both their front office and the
fans, of [Pride Month](https://www.mlb.com/mets/tickets/specials/pride).
Knowing they have so many [queer fans](https://lgbtnetwork.org/mets/), the
Mets celebrate Pride the entire month instead of just one day, and several
players wore Pride Month merchandise and made statements in support of their
gay fans. It was the month that the team, who were terrible up to that point,
really turned it around, and fans started calling them the [Gay
Mets](https://nymag.com/intelligencer/article/gay-grimace-mets-pride-
night.html).

Interestingly, the players seemed to have embraced this as well along with the
ironic memes about Grimace throwing the first pitch and the love for
journeyman second-baseman Jose Iglesias’ song
“[OMG](https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/5579159/2024/06/21/mets-jose-iglesias-
song-omg/).” They began jumping in and out of first place and doing so with a
unique humor that really mirrored the shift in Democratic party’s fortunes
when Kamala Harris and Tim Walz launched a vibes-based campaign of fun and
hope.

2024 was expected to be a rebuilding year for them, allowing them to appear
fated underdogs battling through ecological catastrophe and social chaos to
the NLCS in October, where they finally hit a wall against the Dodgers, just
as the [Harris
campaign](https://ballotpedia.org/Kamala_Harris_presidential_campaign,_2024)
ran out of steam and started sinking in the polls. While they had rediscovered
part of their mission as the Mets of being humorous and whimsical and joyful
and fun and progressive in the face of dour, regressive conservatism, that
wasn’t enough in 2024 to go further.

I write that if members of the team had found some deeper unifying mission,
been more explicitly political, perhaps, by supporting a ceasefire in order
release the Israeli hostages in Gaza, or defending Algerian boxer [Imane
Khelif](https://www.theguardian.com/sport/article/2024/aug/05/olympic-boxer-
in-gender-eligibility-row-hits-out-at-bullies-as-iba-doubles-down) against the
transphobic smears during the Olympics, or protesting the racist and
xenophobic and homophobic Trump ads playing during the playoffs, they might
have found the will fight harder and battle deeper in October, as they had in
1969.

_**Daniel Falcone:** Aside from the more
[conservative](https://archive.nytimes.com/www.nytimes.com/books/first/w/will-
bunts.html),
[traditional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Men_at_Work:_The_Craft_of_Baseball)
or even [nationalistic](https://www.theguardian.com/world/richard-adams-
blog/2010/mar/02/jim-bunning-senate-ted-williams) accounts of baseball that
serve as appeals to patriotism, to what extent are the Mets, and your book, a
reflection of what is good and [constructive
](https://progressive.org/latest/when-baseball-gets-radical-
buhle-220512/)about America and its past? _

**A.M. Gittlitz:** One side of baseball, like America, insists on rigid social
hierarchies and [Social
Darwinist](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/spencer/) ideals of [survival-
of-the-fittest](https://www.britannica.com/science/survival-of-the-fittest).
Another is egalitarian and seeks to break those divisions. The first thing
that was truly remarkable about the
[Mets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z2NAiVa6sOY) was the way the nature of
its “[New Breed](https://www.nytimes.com/1964/08/24/archives/the-new-breed-
and-the-mets-signs-of-the-times.html)” fans challenged received notions of a
reverent, patriotic-like spectatorship, and changed the sport as a result.
Never had a crowd in such big numbers cheered so loudly for a team so bad-an
ironic relationship summarized by the cheer-jeer they invented: “[Let’s go
Mets](https://www.mlb.com/news/video-1986-lets-go-mets/c-67535872)!”

Widespread adaptation of [Mets](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tkTvtYkjFlg)
branding and fan culture marked a new iconoclastic phase for [America’s
Pastime](https://newcriterion.com/article/remembrance-of-swings-past/). The
once grayscale, segregated sport exploded in sound and color. Fans began
expressing themselves more freely, wearing hats and T-shirts of the teams.
Players elected a union militant in [Marvin
Miller](https://www.nytimes.com/2012/11/28/sports/baseball/marvin-miller-
union-leader-who-changed-baseball-dies-at-95.html) to demand greater control
of the game. In [1969](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UmdfLp5G8RI),
[Shea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Shea) saw a revival of a field-
storming tradition dormant since the turn of the century in which fans and
players merged on the field to celebrate together in an orgy of destruction.
The catharsis of professional sports shows us the power of [mass political
participation](https://epicenter.wcfia.harvard.edu/articles/power-sports-
unite-and-divide), which is more powerful when the boundaries of spectacular
society are rejected and transcended.
